Q463.L1t: Geophysics uses indirect methods to study parts of Earth that cannot be reached directly.
Q463.L2t: Earth's magnetic field is generated by motion of molten iron in the outer core and varies over time.
Q463.L3t: Seismic waves change speed and bend or reflect at boundaries between layers of different density and state, and the Earth's interior is deep and hot enough that direct sampling reaches only a tiny fraction of it.
Q463.L4t: Analysis of how fast seismic waves travel and what paths they take through the planet has revealed the most about the core, mantle and lower crust.
Q463.L2f: Earth's magnetic field has stayed constant in strength and direction throughout geologic history, with no reversals.
Q463.L3f: The magnetic field's intensity and fluctuations at the surface directly encode the density and composition of every layer from the crust down through the mantle to the core.
Q463.L4f: Measuring the strength and variations of Earth's magnetic field has given the most information about the core, mantle and lower crust.

Q269.L1t: Teachers use many kinds of classroom strategies to organize discussion and support literacy learning.
Q269.L2t: Concentric circles is a structured speaking activity in which students rotate to face new partners and discuss prompts with each other.
Q269.L3t: To plan instruction for individuals, a teacher needs a tool that records what each student already knows and what each wants to learn, before and after a topic, in a form the teacher can review.
Q269.L4t: A K-W-L chart is the activity that best helps a teacher gather data on individual students' needs.
Q269.L2f: Concentric circles was developed as a standardized written test that is scored by a central testing agency.
Q269.L3f: Concentric circles has each student answer questions in writing alone, giving the teacher a permanent individual record of every student's prior knowledge and learning needs.
Q269.L4f: Concentric circles is the activity that best helps a teacher collect data to inform instruction for individual students.

Q228.L1t: Digital images can be saved in several file formats, each with different ways of storing picture data.
Q228.L2t: JPEG compression is lossy, and repeated saving at high compression can produce visible artifacts such as blockiness.
Q228.L3t: JPEG reduces file size by discarding fine detail that the human eye is less likely to notice, so the discarded information cannot be recovered afterward.
Q228.L4t: A JPEG shrinks file size by selectively throwing away some of the image data.
Q228.L2f: JPEG compression was designed mainly for line drawings and text, and it works poorly on photographs.
Q228.L3f: The JPEG format is built around a color encoding, and it cannot store images that have no color, such as grayscale photos.
Q228.L4f: The JPEG format is used only for color photos.
